questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Pulse against tempo
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the pulse of a piece from its tempo
questions.explanation: The pulse is the underlying steady beat that a listener supplies or hears even when no note lands on it, and it is the thing that lets a group of players stay together. The tempo is how fast that pulse goes, and it is a measurement rather than a thing heard directly: nobody hears ninety beats a minute, they hear a moderately quick beat. The two are separate because a pulse can be fast or slow while staying the same pulse, and a piece can hold one pulse while changing its speed, which is what a composer does at the end of a section to drive towards a climax. The tempting belief is that the two words are synonyms, which is why a student asked to name the tempo of a piece often answers with a description of where the beats fall.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two is the steady underlying beat and which is a measurement of it.

options.text: The pulse is the steady underlying beat, and the tempo is how fast that beat goes
The pulse is the speed of the beat, and the tempo is where the beats fall in the bar
options.misconception: reverses the two, taking tempo to mean the accent pattern instead of the speed

options.text: They are two names for the same quantity, so either word may be used in their place
options.misconception: treats the two terms as synonyms, when one is a beat and one is a rate

options.text: The tempo is fixed for the whole piece, and the pulse is what changes between sections
options.misconception: assumes the speed is constant, when composers routinely change it mid-piece

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The beat and the measure in simple meter
questions.learningObjective: state what a measure collects in simple quadruple metre
questions.explanation: In 4/4 the beat is a quarter note and the measure collects four of them, so the top number of the signature counts the beats and the bottom number names the note that carries the beat. A note shorter than a quarter divides the beat, and a note longer than a quarter spans several beats, so the two levels nest by division and multiplication rather than being two unrelated counts. The measure exists so that a player can tell when to stop counting and start again, and its length is what makes the music able to be looped or phased. The mistake is to read the top number as a count of note values instead of a count of beats, which would make 4/4 hold four eighths rather than four quarters.
questions.hint: Ask what the top number of the signature counts and what the bottom number names.

options.text: The measure collects four quarter-note beats, and shorter notes divide the beat
The measure collects four eighth-note beats, and shorter notes divide the beat
options.misconception: reads the top number as a count of note values rather than a count of beats

options.text: The measure collects one whole note's worth of beats, split four different ways
options.misconception: treats the two numbers as one quantity rather than a count and a note value

options.text: The measure collects however many beats the composer chooses, since 4/4 is a suggestion
options.misconception: believes a time signature is optional, when it fixes the bar length exactly

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The beat unit in compound metre
questions.learningObjective: identify the beat unit of a compound metre
questions.explanation: The signature 6/8 looks like six beats because the top number is a six, but the pulse is felt in two, and each of those two beats is a dotted quarter note that divides into three eighths. The rule is that a compound metre has a top number of six, nine or twelve, and the beat is a dotted note whose three parts are the note named at the bottom. So 6/8 has two beats, 9/8 has three and 12/8 has four, and in each case dividing the beat gives three rather than two. The trap is reading the six as six separate beats, which produces a fast six-beat lilt instead of a slow two-beat sway, and it is the reason a piece marked 6/8 is sometimes counted in six and comes out with the wrong length.
questions.hint: Ask how many parts each beat divides into, and what that implies about the number of beats.

options.text: A dotted quarter note, dividing into three eighths, and there are two beats in the bar
An eighth note, dividing into two sixteenths, and there are six beats in the bar
options.misconception: reads the top number as six beats, which turns a compound metre into a fast simple one

options.text: A quarter note, dividing into two eighths, and there are six beats in the bar
options.misconception: ignores the compound division and takes the bottom number as the beat unit

options.text: A half note, dividing into four quarters, and there are three beats in the bar
options.misconception: picks a beat unit two levels too long for the signature shown

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The total duration of a measure
questions.learningObjective: state the total duration of a measure in 6/8
questions.explanation: The total of one measure is the top number multiplied by the note at the bottom, so 6/8 holds six eighth notes, which comes to three quarter notes, which is also one dotted half note. The number of beats and the total length are different facts and are easily confused: 6/8 has two beats but lasts as long as a 3/4 bar, because both are three quarter notes long. That equality is why a piece can move between the two signatures at a point where the metre is under pressure without changing the total length, which is a standard way to change the accent pattern without changing the amount of music. The mistake is to answer with the beat count, or to multiply the top by the beat unit and get a figure half as large as the truth.
questions.hint: Multiply the top number by the note value at the bottom, then convert to quarter notes.

options.text: Six eighth notes, which is the same length as three quarter notes
Two dotted quarters, which is twice as long as a 3/4 measure of the same tempo
options.misconception: multiplies the top number by the beat rather than by the written note value

options.text: Six quarter notes, reading the bottom number as a quarter rather than an eighth
options.misconception: ignores the note value at the bottom and treats every top number as quarters

options.text: Two beats, which is the pulse count rather than the total length of the bar
options.misconception: reports the number of beats instead of the duration of the measure

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The length of a dotted note
questions.learningObjective: state the duration of a dotted note
questions.explanation: A dot after a note adds half of that note's own value to it, so a dotted quarter is a quarter plus an eighth, which is three eighths, and a dotted half is a half plus a quarter, which is three quarters. The rule is a ratio rather than a fixed amount, so the dot's size follows the note it follows, and that is what lets the dot work in every note value. A second dot adds half of the first dot, giving a double-dotted quarter of one and three quarter notes. The common error is to add a fixed amount regardless of the note, or to add the value of the note above rather than half of it, and both produce a bar that does not add up when the notes are totalled.
questions.hint: Ask what fraction of the note's own value the dot adds, and what that gives for a quarter note.

options.text: It adds half the note's value, so a dotted quarter lasts one and a half beats
It adds a fixed eighth note, so a dotted quarter lasts one and a quarter beats
options.misconception: adds a fixed amount instead of half of the note's own value

options.text: It adds the value of the note above it, so a dotted quarter lasts two beats
options.misconception: adds a whole note above rather than half of the note it follows

options.text: It doubles the note, so a dotted quarter lasts the same as a half note
options.misconception: treats the dot as a second note of the same value, which is what a tie does

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Tie against slur
questions.learningObjective: state what a tie does that a slur does not
questions.explanation: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one sounding length, so the two written values are added and the sound does not restart between them; a slur joins notes of different pitches and asks for them to be played legato, with no change to any duration and a separate attack on each note. The two are easily confused because both are curved lines, and the reliable test is the pitch: same pitch means a tie, different pitches means a slur. A tie also crosses a bar line, which is its commonest practical use, letting a note begun in one measure be held over into the next. A slur never changes how long anything lasts, and a student who thinks it does will mis-tot the bar.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two notes joined by the curve are at the same pitch or at different pitches.

options.text: A tie combines two notes of the same pitch into a single sounding length
A tie joins two notes of different pitches to be played legato and smoothly
options.misconception: gives the tie the job that belongs to a slur, which is a phrasing mark

options.text: A tie shortens the notes it joins, so the beat count of the bar stays the same
options.misconception: believes a tie adjusts the bar rather than lengthening the sound

options.text: A tie applies only to notes in the same measure, never across a bar line
options.misconception: denies the tie's commonest use, which is carrying a note over a bar line

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Rests and their durations
questions.learningObjective: name the rest that fills a given part of a bar
questions.explanation: A rest stands for a measured span of silence, and it lasts exactly as long as a note of the same value would: a whole rest fills a whole bar in 4/4, a half rest fills half a bar, a quarter rest a beat, and an eighth rest half a beat. The naming comes from the value, not from the position in the bar, so a half rest in the first half of a 4/4 bar and one in the second half are the same rest, and only the convention of hanging the whole rest from the fourth line distinguishes it. The error to avoid is reading a rest as an absence rather than as a duration, which leads a student to think a bar with a rest in it is short rather than full.
questions.hint: Ask how many beats the gap occupies, then choose the rest whose value matches that number.

options.text: A half rest, since two beats of silence are filled by a rest of half-note value
A whole rest, since any gap filling part of a bar counts as a full-bar rest
options.misconception: calls any rest a whole rest regardless of how long the gap actually is

options.text: A quarter rest, since the gap is described as being between beats rather than on them
options.misconception: infers the value from the gap's position rather than from its length

options.text: A dotted half rest, which is the only rest that can sit between two beats
options.misconception: invents a value no rest carries, and places it by position not duration

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Syncopation and displaced accent
questions.learningObjective: describe where the accent falls in a syncopated passage
questions.explanation: Syncopation is the displacement of the accent away from the beat on which the metre puts it, so the emphasis lands between the beats or on a weak beat that is held over into a strong one. In 4/4 the first beat is the strongest and the third is the next, so a figure that makes the second beat the longest note of the bar is syncopated, and so is one that ties a weak beat across the bar line into the downbeat. The underlying pulse does not change: the listener still counts one two three four, but the music contradicts where the weight ought to be, and the resulting tension is what gives syncopation its bite. The error is to think syncopation means the metre has been altered, rather than that the accent has been moved against an unchanged metre.
questions.hint: Ask where the metre puts the strongest beat, and then where the music actually places its emphasis.

options.text: The accent falls between the beats or on a weak beat held over, against an unchanged pulse
The accent stays on the first beat throughout, so nothing about the accent has moved
options.misconception: believes syncopation leaves the accent where the metre puts it

options.text: The accent is placed equally on all four beats, so no beat stands out at all
options.misconception: confuses syncopation with an even accent, which is the opposite condition

options.text: The accent falls off the metre entirely, so the listener stops counting one two three four
options.misconception: assumes the underlying pulse is abandoned rather than contradicted

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The ratio a tuplet implies
questions.learningObjective: state the ratio a triplet implies
questions.explanation: A tuplet fits a stated number of notes into the time normally taken by a different number, and the triplet is the commonest case: three notes in the time of two, written 3 against 2. In 4/4 a beat is one quarter note, so three triplet eighths fill that one quarter, which makes each of them a third of a beat rather than the half a beat an ordinary eighth would get. Other tuplets state their own ratio: a duplet puts two in the time of three, a quadruplet four in the time of three, and a quintuplet five in the time of four. The mistake is to think a triplet makes three notes take the time of three, which would be no change at all and is why the written number has to be shown next to the normal one.
questions.hint: Ask how many notes are written and how many of the ordinary kind they are fitted into.

options.text: Three notes in the time of two, written 3 against 2 so each is shortened
Three notes in the time of three, which leaves each note at its ordinary length
options.misconception: thinks a triplet changes nothing, so the figure would be redundant

options.text: Three notes in the time of four, which stretches them rather than shortening them
options.misconception: takes the tuplet as a lengthening, when the notes are fitted more tightly

options.text: Two notes in the time of three, which is the ratio the duplet actually uses
options.misconception: gives the duplet's ratio, which fits two notes into three rather than three into two

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Hemiola and regrouped beats
questions.learningObjective: describe the grouping a hemiola creates
questions.explanation: A hemiola overlays a grouping of three on a grouping of two, and in 6/8 it appears as three groups of two eighths set against the meter's usual two groups of three. The eighths are unchanged in total length, so the bar still holds six of them and the tempo does not change; what changes is where the weight falls, from two long beats to three shorter ones. That produces a momentary cross-rhythm, and because the two readings are both legitimate ways of hearing the same six notes, the passage sounds as though it has slipped against the metre. The error is to treat a hemiola as a change of time signature or a doubling of the tempo, when nothing about the notation or the total duration has altered at all.
questions.hint: Ask how many groups of two eighth notes are being heard against the meter's own grouping.

options.text: Three groups of two eighths set against the meter's two groups of three
Six groups of one eighth, which removes the meter's grouping altogether
options.misconception: believes the hemiola dissolves the underlying grouping rather than overlaying a second one

options.text: Two groups of four eighths, which doubles the length of the meter's own beats
options.misconception: doubles the beat length, which would double the length of the bar as well

options.text: A change of tempo, so the bar takes twice as long as it did before
options.misconception: reads a regrouping of the same notes as a change of speed

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Polyphony against homophony
questions.learningObjective: distinguish polyphony from homophony
questions.explanation: The distinction is about how independently the voices move. In homophony there is a melody and the other parts support it, moving largely in the same rhythm, so the harmony changes under a single tune. In polyphony the parts carry their own melodies, each with its own rhythm and its own points of emphasis, so no voice is subordinate in the way a accompaniment is. The test is whether a voice could be extracted and still sound like a tune, which it can in a fugue and usually cannot in a harmonised hymn tune. The error is to read polyphony as a matter of how many parts there are, since a four-part hymn with a moving bass is polyphonic in its way and a two-part invention with two equal lines is not merely simpler polyphony but simply polyphony.
questions.hint: Ask whether the parts share a rhythm or each carry their own melodic line.

options.text: In polyphony the parts move independently, and in homophony they share a melody's rhythm
In polyphony the parts share a rhythm, and in homophony each carries its own line
options.misconception: reverses the two, which is the standard first error in this pair

options.text: Polyphony is the style with more parts, and homophony is the style with fewer
options.misconception: reads the difference as a matter of part count rather than of independence

options.text: Polyphony is always faster than homophony, and homophony is always slower
options.misconception: confuses a rhythmic category with a tempo, which is a separate property

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Monophonic, two-part and fugal texture
questions.learningObjective: identify a two-part texture
questions.explanation: The categories are defined by how many independent lines there are and how they relate. Monophonic means a single line with nothing else sounding. Two-part means exactly two lines, each with its own material, and it is the smallest texture in which the parts can imitate, contradict or combine with each other. Fugal texture is a many-voiced form of polyphony in which one voice states a subject and the others take it in turn, each with a line of its own, so it is defined by the entry of a shared subject rather than by the number of voices. The error is to read the labels as a size scale running from one to three, since a two-part invention and a four-part fugue are not two points on one axis but two different kinds of thing.

options.text: Three lines sound at once, since a two-part texture is named for its spacing
options.misconception: reads two-part as a matter of spacing rather than of the number of lines

options.text: Two lines sound, but only because a fugue always begins with two voices

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The interval at which a canon enters
questions.learningObjective: state what fixes the interval at which a canon's second voice enters
questions.explanation: A canon takes a melody and makes it the material for every voice, with each later voice entering on the same melody at a chosen interval and a chosen time after the first. The interval is a composer's decision, not a property of the melody, so a canon can be at the unison, at the octave or at any interval in between, and each choice changes the character: entering at the octave sounds like an echo of the same line, while entering at a fifth or a sixth puts the two lines in different registers and against each other harmonically. The delay in time is a second free choice, and it is what makes the imitation audible as imitation rather than as coincidence. The error is to think the interval is fixed by the key or the metre, which it is not.
questions.hint: Ask whether the interval between the voices is a property of the melody or a choice made by the composer.

options.text: It is a chosen interval, and each choice changes how the two lines sound against each other
It is fixed by the key signature, so a canon in a sharp key sits a fifth apart
options.misconception: believes the signature determines the interval, which it does not

options.text: It is fixed by the metre, so the interval matches the number of beats in the bar
options.misconception: believes the metre determines the interval between the entering voices

options.text: It is always the octave, since a canon is by definition an imitation at the octave
options.misconception: takes one common choice to be the only possible one

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Sequences and their transposing interval
questions.learningObjective: define a sequence and name its transposing interval
questions.explanation: A sequence restates a figure at a different pitch level, and the interval of transposition is the distance the figure has been moved, so naming a sequence means naming that interval. A descending-fifths sequence, the commonest in tonal music, moves the figure down a fifth, which on the circle of fifths means each repetition adds a sharp, and that is exactly why the sequence keeps modulating while sounding coherent. A sequence at the same interval every time is called a real sequence, and one whose interval changes at each step is called an irregular or tonal sequence, which is a freer device. The error is to treat a repeated figure in the same key and register as a sequence, since a sequence must move; and to describe a sequence only by the fact of repetition, which would include an exact repeat.
questions.hint: Ask what has to change for a repetition of a figure to count as a sequence.

The figure is restated at exactly the same pitches, which is what makes it a sequence

options.text: The figure is restated in another key, so the interval does not need to be the same
options.misconception: makes a change of key the definition, ignoring the transposition itself

options.text: The figure is restated at a new tempo, so the intervals between its notes stretch
options.misconception: confuses a change of speed with a change of pitch level in the figure

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Rondo form and its refrain
questions.learningObjective: identify the recurring section of a rondo
questions.explanation: A rondo is defined by a refrain that keeps coming back, and by contrast material that does not. The simple rondo is usually written ABACA, with the refrain A three times and two episodes B and C between them; the grand rondo lengthens this to ABACADA, adding a second refrain D and giving five returns. What makes the form a rondo rather than any other alternation is that the same section recurs, and the episodes are written so that each return of the refrain is heard as a homecoming rather than as a repeat of something that has not changed. The error is to call the episode the returning section, since the episodes appear once each by definition and it is the refrain that recurs.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two kinds of section appears more than once in the outline.

The episode, which returns between the refrains and holds the form together

options.text: The bridge, which appears twice and separates the two main sections of the piece
options.misconception: borrows a term from popular music for a section a rondo does not use

options.text: The coda, which comes last and closes the work after the final refrain
options.misconception: picks the closing section, which appears once and is optional besides

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Binary and ternary form
questions.learningObjective: recognise a ternary formal outline
questions.explanation: Ternary form is defined by a return: the first section, a contrasting second section, and then the first material again, which is written A B A. The return is what makes it ternary rather than binary, since a binary movement has two sections and no return, and it is usually the first section that returns rather than the second. The return may be shortened or altered, and it is often expanded at the end so the piece can widen out into a proper close, so the third section need not be an exact copy. A rounded binary, A B A', adds a return to a binary plan and sits between the two, and it is the commonest shape in dance movements of the period.

Binary, because there are only two different kinds of material in the movement

options.misconception: calls any recurring section a refrain, which is a rondo term

options.text: Continuous, because no bar line marks where one section hands over to the next

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Theme and variations
questions.learningObjective: state what must remain constant in a set of variations
questions.explanation: A set of variations presents a theme and then a series of versions of it, and what the listener must still recognise in each version is the theme itself, its melodic shape and its order of events. Everything else is fair game: the harmony, the metre, the tempo, the key, the orchestration, the note values and the length of each variation. The device depends on a listener being able to hear the same tune inside a changed surface, and if the tune itself is replaced the form has become something else, such as a set of unrelated pieces placed after each other. A variation that alters the theme's intervals while keeping its rhythm is a recognised technique, so the constant that matters is recognisability rather than literal repetition of every note.
questions.hint: Ask what a listener must still be able to recognise in each version for the set to be a set of variations.

options.text: The theme itself, which must stay recognisable while its surface changes around it
The key, since a variation that changed key would not belong to the same movement
options.misconception: treats the key as fixed, although modulating variations are common

options.text: The tempo, since the theme is a tune and a tune implies a single speed for it
options.misconception: holds the speed fixed, though tempo changes are a standard variation

options.text: The instrumentation, since the theme is defined by the sound that first played it
options.misconception: believes the theme lives in one instrument, which is a performance fact

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: A fugue's answer against its subject
questions.learningObjective: describe how a fugue's answer differs from its subject
questions.explanation: The subject is the tune stated by the first voice, and the answer is what the second voice sings in reply. It is not the same tune transposed, because the answer is adjusted to fit the new key: any interval in the subject that would fall on a note outside the new key is altered, most often by moving it by a step, and the adjustment is what keeps the answer sounding like the same tune. The answer is also normally given on the dominant, the fifth degree, so that the opening establishes the key and its first contrast, and the two voices together set up the tritone between them. Because the answer is a reply rather than a copy, a student who expects a literal transposition has not accounted for the alterations, and one who expects an inversion has confused the answer with a mirror canon.
questions.hint: Ask what the answer must do to the subject's notes that would not fit the new key.

options.text: It is transposed to the dominant and adjusted where a note would not fit the new key
It is the subject transposed exactly, with every interval left as it was written
options.misconception: expects a literal transposition, ignoring the adjustments the reply needs

options.text: It is the subject inverted, with every interval turned upside down around a fixed note
options.misconception: confuses the answer with an inverted canon, which is a different device

options.text: It is the subject played backwards, so that the two voices interlock retrogradally
options.misconception: confuses the answer with a retrograde, which is not a fugue device

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The sections of sonata form
questions.learningObjective: name the main sections of sonata form
questions.explanation: Sonata form has three main sections. The exposition presents two themes, the first in the tonic and the second on the dominant, with a transition joining them, so the two halves of the key are set side by side. The development takes the material away from the tonic and works it through other keys without settling. The recapitulation brings both themes back, and the crucial change is that the second theme now arrives in the tonic rather than the dominant, which resolves the tension the exposition set up. A coda may follow, but it is an addition rather than one of the three. The error is to name a prelude or a coda as one of the main sections, or to say the recapitulation repeats the exposition unchanged, since moving the second theme is the point of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the three main sections are and what changes when the themes come back.

options.text: Exposition, development and recapitulation, with the second theme returning in the tonic
Prelude, fugue and coda, which are the three standard sections of the form
options.misconception: borrows three real section names that are not sonata form's own

options.text: Introduction, exposition and coda, with the development counted as part of the coda
options.misconception: folds the development into the coda, which is a closing addition

options.text: Exposition, development and recapitulation, with both themes returning on the dominant
options.misconception: leaves the second theme on the dominant, which is what the exposition did

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a listener hears the end of a movement
questions.learningObjective: state how a listener recognises the end of a movement
questions.explanation: A movement ends at a cadence, and the sign that a cadence has arrived is a combination of harmonic closure and rhythmic settling: a progression that resolves onto the tonic, usually from the dominant, together with a phrase whose length and motion finally stop rather than continue. The cadence point is where that resolution happens, and a listener usually feels it as a change of tension a fraction before being able to name it. The strongest closure is the perfect authentic cadence, where both chords are in root position and the melody lands on the tonic, so the ear is given the arrival in the harmony, in the bass and in the tune at once. The error is to look for a formal signal instead, such as a change of tempo or a thinning of the texture, either of which may coincide with the end but neither of which is the cadence.
questions.hint: Ask what harmonic event tells the listener the music has stopped moving, and where the melody lands.

options.text: At a cadence, where the harmony resolves and the rhythmic motion finally settles
Whenever the tempo changes, since a change of speed marks every formal boundary
options.misconception: treats a change of tempo as a boundary marker, which need not coincide with one

options.text: Whenever the texture thins out, since fewer voices means the music is finishing
options.misconception: reads a change of density as a sign of the end, which composers use at other points

options.text: Whenever the melody reaches its highest note, since that is where the tension peaks
options.misconception: confuses the climax with the close, which are different structural events

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Modulation and the pivot chord
questions.learningObjective: identify the pivot chord in a passage that modulates
questions.explanation: The pivot is the chord on G. The three notes sounding there are G, B and D, and those notes form a G major triad. In C major, G is the fifth degree, so a G major triad is the dominant. In D major the same triad is built on the fourth degree, because the D major scale is D, E, F sharp, G, A, B, C sharp, and the triad standing on G is G, B, D, which is the subdominant. So one chord is the dominant of C and the subdominant of D at the same time, and that is exactly what a pivot chord has to be. The confirmation comes from what follows: the passage moves to A major, which is the dominant of D, and then to D itself, so the last three chords are read as subdominant, dominant and tonic in the new key. The chord on A is not a pivot, because it needs a C sharp and so belongs to D major only.
questions.hint: Ask which of the chords can be built from the notes of both of the two keys, then check what follows it.

options.text: G major, which is the dominant of C major and the subdominant of D major at once
A major, which is the dominant of D major and also belongs to C major as it stands
options.misconception: claims a chord built on A is diatonic to C major, when it would need a C sharp

options.text: D major, since the pivot must be the tonic that the passage finally arrives on
options.misconception: takes the pivot to be the new tonic, which arrives only after the reinterpretation

options.text: There is no pivot chord, because a single chord can belong to only one key at a time
options.misconception: denies that one chord can be diatonic to two keys at the same moment

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: Comparing the length of a bar
questions.learningObjective: compare the length of bars across different time signatures
questions.explanation: The length of a bar is the top number multiplied by the note at the bottom, so the four bars measure one and a half, two, three and five quarter notes, and one and a half is the smallest. The 3/8 bar holds three eighths, which is one and a half quarters. The 2/4 bar holds a quarter and two eighths, which is one plus one, so two. The 3/4 bar holds three quarters. The 6/4 bar holds a dotted half and a half, which is three plus two, so five. The second check converts every bar into eighths: three, four, six and ten, and three is the smallest of those. The trap is reading the top number as the length, which would make 6/4 look like the shortest bar, the opposite of the truth.
questions.hint: Convert each bar into eighths using its signature and its written contents, then compare the four totals.

questions.topic: The total duration of a 6/8 measure
questions.learningObjective: state the total duration of a measure in 6/8 in quarter notes
questions.explanation: Multiplying the top number by the note at the bottom gives six eighths, and each eighth is half a quarter, so the total is three quarter notes. The second route converts the other way, since three quarter notes are three pairs of eighths, which is six eighths, confirming the same figure. Both agree, and the figure is worth stating in quarter notes because it is the only way to see that a 6/8 bar and a 3/4 bar last the same amount of time while carrying a different number of beats. The error is to answer with the beat count, which is two and not three, or to treat the bottom number as a quarter and answer six.

The error is to round to four or to answer nine by treating the bottom number as a quarter.

The second route works in whole notes: a half note is half a whole note, so three of them are one and a half whole notes, and a whole note is four quarters, so one and a half wholes are six quarters. Both routes agree. The signature 3/2 carries three beats of two quarter notes each, so it has the same number of beats as 3/4 and twice the length, which is exactly the kind of pair a composer uses to make a passage feel broader without changing the pulse at all.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The length of a dotted quarter
questions.learningObjective: state the length of a dotted quarter in quarter notes
questions.explanation: A dot adds half of the note's own value, so a dotted quarter is a quarter plus an eighth, which is one and a half quarter notes. The second route counts sixteenths: a quarter is four sixteenths and an eighth is two, so a dotted quarter is six sixteenths, and six sixteenths is one and a half quarters. Both agree, and the figure is the beat of every compound duple metre, since 6/8 and 6/4 are both felt in beats of a dotted quarter and a dotted half respectively. The error is to add a whole quarter instead of half of one, giving two, which is the length of a half note and would overflow the bar it is placed in.
questions.hint: Add half of the note's own value to the note, and confirm by counting sixteenths.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: The length of a dotted eighth
questions.learningObjective: state the length of a dotted eighth in quarter notes
questions.explanation: An eighth note is half a quarter, and the dot adds half of the eighth, which is a sixteenth worth a quarter of a quarter, giving three quarters of a quarter note in total. The second route counts in sixteenths: a dotted eighth is three sixteenths, and a sixteenth is a quarter of a quarter, so three sixteenths are three quarters of a quarter. Both routes agree, and the figure is the length of one of the three subdivisions inside a dotted-quarter beat, which is why a dotted eighth is the note a composer reaches for when filling one of those gaps in compound metre. The error is to double the eighth instead of adding half of it, giving a whole quarter, which is four sixteenths rather than three.

questions.topic: The length of a double-dotted half
questions.learningObjective: state the length of a double-dotted half in quarter notes
questions.explanation: A half note is two quarter notes, the first dot adds half of the half, which is one quarter, and the second dot adds half of the first dot, which is half a quarter, giving two plus one plus half, that is three and a half. The second route confirms it in eighths: a double-dotted half is a half of four eighths, plus two eighths, plus one eighth, which is seven eighths, and seven eighths is three and a half quarters. Both agree, and the half that remains is what makes a double-dotted note valuable: it gives a duration that fills a bar of 7/8 exactly, which is a metre built from groups of three and two eighths and so is not a multiple of three. The error is to add a third of the value for the second dot, which would give a total of three and two thirds.

questions.topic: Two notes joined by a tie
questions.learningObjective: state the combined length of two notes joined by a tie
questions.explanation: A tie joins two notes of the same pitch into one sounding length, so the two written values are added: an eighth is half a quarter and a quarter is one, giving one and a half quarter notes. The second route counts sixteenths: an eighth is two and a quarter is four, so six sixteenths in total, and six sixteenths is one and a half quarters. Both agree, and the important point is that the sound does not restart, so the pair is heard as a single note of that length rather than as two notes. The error is to treat a tie as a slur and answer with the second value only, on the grounds that a slur changes no durations at all, which is exactly the confusion the arithmetic exposes.

questions.topic: The length of a half rest
questions.learningObjective: state the length of a half rest in quarter notes
questions.explanation: A rest lasts exactly as long as a note of the same value, so a half rest lasts as long as a half note, which is two quarter notes. The second route checks it against the bar it sits in: in 4/4 a half rest fills half the measure, and a 4/4 measure is four quarters, so half of four is two. Both agree, and the check is the more useful one because it ties the rest's value to the metre rather than to a table. The error is to answer four, treating any rest as a full-bar rest, or to answer one on the grounds that rests are gaps rather than durations, which is the belief that has to be unlearned first.

questions.topic: How a tempo marking becomes a duration
questions.learningObjective: convert a tempo marking into the length of a passage
questions.explanation: A tempo marking states how many beats go by in a minute, so the length of a passage in seconds is the number of beats divided by the tempo and multiplied by sixty. Eight measures of 4/4 contain eight times four, that is thirty-two beats, and thirty-two divided by one hundred and twenty is a little under a third of a minute, which times sixty is sixteen seconds. The second route works at the tempo directly: one hundred and twenty beats a minute is two beats a second, so thirty-two beats take sixteen seconds. Both give sixteen, and the second is the quicker check once the tempo is a round number. The error is dividing by sixty instead of multiplying, or forgetting that 4/4 has four beats to the bar rather than one.
questions.hint: Count the total beats, divide by the beats per minute to get the fraction of a minute, then multiply by sixty.

questions.topic: The beat count of a 6/8 measure
questions.learningObjective: state how many beats a measure of 6/8 contains
questions.explanation: In a compound metre the top number is divided by three, and six divided by three is two, so 6/8 has two beats per measure. Both give two, and the figure is the reason a 6/8 bar is felt as a slow sway rather than a quick six, since each of the two beats is itself three eighths long. The error is to report six, which is the top number rather than the number of beats and turns the compound metre into a fast simple one.

questions.learningObjective: trace a running total of note values in a bar

questions.topic: Why a hemiola feels like a jolt
questions.learningObjective: explain why a hemiola creates a jolt in a compound metre
questions.explanation: The jolt comes from a clash between two readings of the same six notes. In 6/8 the metre establishes two beats, each a dotted quarter divided into three eighths, and that grouping is felt from the first bar onwards. A hemiola overlays three groups of two eighths on those two groups of three, and the total is unchanged, so nothing in the notation announces a change and the tempo does not move. The listener is therefore asked to accept a second, equally coherent division of the same material, and the two readings pull against each other because each one wants to be the downbeat. The result is a momentary sense of acceleration or of dislocation, followed by a snap back to the metre when the hemiola stops. The belief to correct is that a hemiola is a change of metre or of speed: it is a change of grouping only, which is why the bar still contains six eighths afterwards.

The total is unchanged and nothing in the notation signals a change, so the tempo never moves; what moves is where the weight falls. Because each reading wants its own grouping to be the downbeat, the ear is pulled between them and the passage sounds momentarily faster or dislocated until the hemiola ends and the metre reasserts itself. questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a fugue's answer is built
questions.learningObjective: explain how a fugue's answer differs from its subject and why
questions.explanation: The answer is the subject transposed, and then adjusted, and the adjustment is the whole reason it is not a copy. The second voice normally enters on the dominant, the fifth degree, so the tune is moved a fifth away from where it started. A literal transposition would often put one of the subject's notes outside the new key, since the intervals of the tune were written to fit the first key, so any such note is altered, most often by moving it a step, and the result still has to sound like the same tune to the ear. The double purpose is worth stating: the answer establishes the dominant so that the opening of the fugue sets the key against its first contrast, and it also sets up the tritone between the two voices, which is the interval that will later drive the modulation to the exposition's close. The belief to correct is that an answer is a mirror or a retrograde, both of which are devices a composer may use but neither of which is what defines the answer.

questions.subject: MUSIC_THEORY
questions.topic: How a pivot chord enables a modulation
questions.learningObjective: explain how a pivot chord enables a modulation
questions.explanation: A modulation is easier to hear when it costs no new material, and a pivot chord is the device that arranges this. Take a chord that belongs to both keys at once: in C major the notes G, B and D are the dominant triad, and the same three notes in D major are the triad on the sixth degree, the submediant. The composer sounds the chord first with its C major meaning, so the ear has already accepted those notes as part of C, and then moves the bass and the surrounding chords in a way that makes the same notes function as the submediant of D. Because nothing new has been introduced, the ear accepts the re-reading before it has consciously noticed it, and that is why a pivot can carry a modulation that a listener reports as having happened without being able to say when. The spelling may even change at the point of the reinterpretation, which is a sign the composer is steering the move rather than stumbling into it.

questions.explanation: The order is exposition, development, recapitulation, and then a coda if the movement has one. The exposition presents the two themes, the development takes the material away from the tonic, and the recapitulation brings it back with the second theme now in the tonic rather than the dominant. The coda is an addition after the main three and is optional, so a movement that ends at the recapitulation is complete without it, and that is why it appears last rather than being counted as a fourth main section. The error is to move the development last, which would mean the themes are stated, restated, and only then worked out, and which is not the order any of these sections performs its work in.
questions.hint: Ask which section states the material, which works it out, which brings it home, and which is the optional addition.

questions.learningObjective: order the sections of a rondo outline
questions.explanation: The simple rondo outline is A B A C A, in which the refrain A comes first, an episode follows, the refrain returns, a second and different episode appears, and the refrain closes the movement. The return of the refrain after each episode is what makes the form a rondo rather than any other alternation, and the fact that the two episodes are different material is what stops the shape being a simple repetition. The grand rondo lengthens the same plan by adding a second refrain, giving A B A C A D A, but the underlying rule does not change. The error to avoid is a placement that puts two episodes back to back, since a rondo alternates refrain and episode rather than grouping the contrast material together.
questions.hint: Ask which label is the refrain and check that no two episodes are adjacent in the outline.
